items.summary: Alcohol put her to dangerous situations and filled her with shame. She found a way out. Photo – Robin F.

items.title: Michelle “I’m grateful that Grapevine is around.”
items.summary: After a rocky start, she discovered that a grateful heart doesn’t want to drink. Photo – Michael C.

items.title: Pat D. “It’s a wonderful life here in AA.”
items.summary: The only time he ever turned down a drink was when he “misunderstood the question.” Photo – Jeanna T.

items.title: Abiud - Una triste realidad
items.summary: Un amigo le transmite el mensaje de recuperación y llega a su primera reunión a los 16 años, pero se niega a aceptar su problema con la bebida. Llegá el día en que desesperado se arrodilla y le pide a Dios que lo ayude a dejar de beber, y sucede el milagro. AA y el servicio se convierten en su recuperación. Photo Credit: Justin E.

items.title: Alberto - La decisión
items.summary: Resentido con sus padres por su abandono y consumido por sus miedos e inseguridades, Alberto recurre al alcohol para enfrentar sus temores y darse valor. En un momento de claridad, viendo a su hijo en peligro, toma la decisión de dejar de beber y llega a AA. Photo Credit: Becki W.

items.title: Anselmo M. - Mi mejor amigo
items.summary: Se casó a los doce años con la botella, y desde entonces, Anselmo vivía una vida de egoísmo y resentimientos, haciendo lo que fuera necesario con tal de conseguir alcohol. El alcohol se convierte en su enemigo hasta que se entrega por completo al programa de Alcohólicos Anónimos. Photo Credit: Jeanna T.

items.title: David R. - Llegué a creer
items.summary: David llega a AA a los 21 años resentido con su violento padre, pero encuentra esperanza escuchando a otros alcohólicos compartir su experiencia, esperanza y fortaleza, y llega a creer que él también podía recuperarse y que nunca es demasiado tarde para cambiar su vida. Photo Credit: A. Murphy

items.title: Edgar M. - Una nueva vida
items.summary: Ante la amenaza de su esposa de abandonarlo si no deja de beber, Edgar decide ir a Alcohólicos Anónimos, y ahí, junto a su esposa que se convierte en su apoyo, comienza el camino de la sobriedad. Ahora, lo más importante para él es: pasar el mensaje a otro alcohólico. Photo Credit: Becki W.

items.title: Elmer D. - El mensajero
items.summary: Descripción: Para Elmer una vida sin alcohol era inimaginable, bebía sin parar y termina viviendo en la calle pidiendo dinero para comprar alcohol. Una “goma” moral lo hace recapacitar y su Poder Superior lo lleva a AA. Photo Credit: Carole B.

items.title: Eloy E. - De la oscuridad a la luz
items.summary: Dominado por los resentimientos, Eloy descubre el alcohol a los 13 años y con ello una sensación de paz, alegría y tranquilidad. Con esa sensación se despertó el diablillo que llevaba adentro, al que llamaba “resentimiento hacia mi padre”. En el programa se libera de ese resentimiento, que era la barrera a su recuperación, y su padre se convierte en su mejor amigo. Photo Credit: Eric S.

items.title: Hugo L. - Milagros
items.summary: Descripción: Comienza a beber desde muy temprana edad y desde la primera vez no pudo, ni quiso parar. Vive una vida ingobernable hasta que llega a AA impulsado por un gran miedo a lo que le podría pasar si continuaba bebiendo así. Dios y AA hacen milagros y Hugo logra mantenerse sobrio un día a la vez. Photo Credit: Michael C.

items.title: José C. - Mi infancia, mi alcoholismo y mi recuperación
items.summary: José descubre el alcohol y de ser un estudiante con aspiraciones se convierte en un borracho sin esperanzas. Pierde a su familia y su alcoholismo convierte su sueño americano en una pesadilla. Photo Credit: R. Hamm

items.title: Manuel R. - El privilegio
items.summary: Borracho todos los días y hasta durmiendo en los parques, Manuel se convierte en una persona indeseable dentro de la sociedad; creía que su destino era morir borracho, pero su Poder Superior tenía otros planes para él, y le regala el privilegio de llevar el mensaje a otros alcohólicos. Photo Credit: Drew S.

items.title: Cal “We’ve been dancing together ever since.”
items.summary: When they were drinking, Cal and his wife loved to dance—but they were dance partners in the disease of alcoholism. Photo Credit: A. Conway

items.title: Emma A. “I’ve been coming to Step One as far back as I can remember.”
items.summary: She grew up feeling distant from friends and family, isolated both by alcoholism and her then-hidden identity as a trans woman. Finally, in a moment of clarity, she understood that “to survive I had to put down the drink.” Photo Credit: A. Conway

items.title: Jim T. “Finally, I really was sick and tired.”
items.summary: Jim came into AA, but kept on drinking between meetings. He watched his family began to fall apart and he saw that he might lose everything unless he became honest with himself and others. Photo Credit: J. Graham

items.title: Jody “I had no doubt that I was exactly where I was supposed to be.”
items.summary: Forty-one felonies later, she ended up in prison where a chance remark during an AA meeting led her to a spiritual experience. Photo Credit: B.Willman

items.title: Linda-Ann “I knew my Dad would love AA.”
items.summary: She was told to focus on her own recovery, not her father’s—but through a variety of strategies, she helped him to enjoy long-term sobriety. Photo Credit: Joe L.

items.title: Liz “Nobody really cared. They were just happy to see me.”
items.summary: During her first 90 days after a relapse she was flying solo—“mistake number one”—before the women in her group gathered around her. Photo Credit: C. Tremblay

items.title: Rodney W. “A messenger to save the lives of others.”
items.summary: His mother took out an insurance policy on him because she didn’t think he would live until the age of 30. While drinking, he dreamed of “a better place” away from pain and despair. That place, it turned out, was AA. Photo Credit: C. Tremblay

items.title: Sandy “There is nothing more important in my life than Alcoholics Anonymous”
items.summary: From an upper middle class family to detox and the Salvation Army, she found her way to a new life and a happy retirement by doing “all the things that AA teaches us to do.” Photo Credit: M. Tipper

Es un servicio fundamental para La Viña, ya que el RLV vincula a los miembros de la comunidad con un servicio y herramienta del Paso Doce. Tú como RLV puedes marcar la diferencia para aquellos que ni siquiera saben que AA tiene una revista…

items.title: Marsha P. “Change or die.”
items.summary: Marsha’s first sponsor was the picture of unmanageability—four kids from three different fathers, a chaotic household. But Marsha always felt warmed and accepted by her character and her wisdom, even if Marsha could never quite find the words to ask her officially to be her sponsor. Photo Credit: S. Driedger

items.title: Haley H. “Don’t let anyone ever say you don’t belong here.”
items.summary: As a transgender woman with seven months sober, Haley was feeling rejected by the home group she had decided to adopt. After one meeting, she was hurried out the door, literally on her way to get a drink, but met the man who would become her sponsor—sent, she believes, by her Higher Power Photocredit: B.Willman

items.title: Scott M. “Finding my father.”
items.summary: With decades of strong sobriety, Scott decided he wanted to get close to his ill and aging father, who had kept him at arm’s length throughout their lives. Yet he could never crack the barrier, until his sponsor suggested that Scott needed to change, because his father was unlikely to. This realization brought effected a true transformation in their relationship. Photocredit: K. Cook

items.title: Ken M. “Forget everything you thought you knew.”
items.summary: When Ken took his first drink after a tough childhood and a motorcycle accident at the age of 18, he found an illusory freedom and happiness. Twenty years later, cycling in and out of A.A., he met a sponsor who advised him that his old way of thinking was keeping him drunk. Photocredit: B.Willman

items.title: Byron B. “The solution wasn’t me.” - AA Grapevine
items.summary: “They didn’t say keep coming back. They said don’t come back.” One Thanksgiving, Byron found himself completely alone—rejected by his family, even his church group, because of the trail of devastation his drinking had left behind. His sponsor told him to let go of pride and let the program in. Photocredit: K. Cook #alcoholicsanonymous #aa #twelvesteps #drinking #aagrapevine #quitdrinking…

items.title: Kathy R. “I was surrounded.”
items.summary: Kathy’s idea of intimacy was: “Come here, come here, go away, go away.” But when she walked into her first meeting she was surrounded by sober women—and decided she wanted what they had. These women included her sponsor who helped Kathy with what she most needed: the Steps. Photo Credit: S. Driedger

items.title: PS. W. “Not my business.”
items.summary: Going to meetings and continuing to drink? PS describes it as an “awful crossroads in my life,” but finally understood that willpower wasn’t the answer. She called her sponsor about every drink trigger, from traffic jams to not getting her way at home. There was a simple phrase her sponsor repeated that got her through those first, tough 90 days. Photo Credit: J. Thacker

items.title: Myra G. “Whatever you do, be honest.” - AA Grapevine
items.summary: Thirty days into sobriety, Myra got an interview for her dream job. One problem: her DWI arrest, two years before. She was sure she needed to lie to get the job, but before the interview she decided to ask her sponsor for advice. It was a good thing she did. Photo Credit: J.
